title: After My Clerkship at Freiburg University
paragraphs: Through the fiscal 2016 overseas clinical clerkship program, I was given the opportunity to study for three months at Freiburg University in Freiburg, an environmental city in southwestern Germany. It is rather sudden, but I am the type of person who becomes utterly fascinated by origins and the like, and out of a somewhat childish interest, thinking "I often hear that Japanese medicine came from Germany, and I am told that the charts of old Japanese doctors were in German! So I am vaguely interested," I wanted to go and study in Germany, and that was the starting point for my application, and I was happy to be given the opportunity. I had known about this program since before entering university, and at that time America seemed to be the forefront of medicine, so I had only a vague feeling that I wanted to go to America, but as described above, by the time of the application period it had changed to wanting to study in Germany. For this there were reasons: given the department I aspire to, I probably would not have many chances to go to Germany in the future (I do not know whether this is true, but I judged so at the time of application); and America I will probably have chances to go to later for conference presentations and the like, and I wanted to visit it after my future career is fixed, saying "I want to study or research such-and-such." So, as a student, at this time just before becoming a doctor, I wanted above all to study in Germany, the root of Japanese medicine, and I took part in this program.

In this study abroad, I trained in cardiac surgery and orthopedics (trauma surgery) at Freiburg University Hospital, and in general surgery and anesthesiology at the Diakoniekrankenhaus, a community hospital near the university hospital. Let me add a note here from the viewpoint of German medical education: medical schools in Germany are six-year programs like Japan's, but the system of clerkships and so on is a little different. In the fifth year, as with polyclinic clerkships in Japan, students rotate through several departments for a few weeks each, and in the sixth year they train in a department and hospital of their own choosing while receiving a small salary, spending their time in a state that is, so to speak, between a resident and a student. Because they actually work in the hospital, they are well versed in drug and injection doses, and in anesthesiology the students actually administered drugs as well. Knowing in what kind of system overseas medical students learn was also one of my original aims, so I was glad to be able to catch a glimpse of this by training with the local medical students. Now I will describe each clerkship.

First, from 4/4 I rotated through general surgery for four weeks. The content was that after gathering in the morning we did light rounds, then held a conference where we discussed the day's operating schedule and consults on the previous day's ER cases. When speaking with patients and in conferences, everything was in German, and I struggled to grasp the content during this time, and asked the doctors about what I did not understand. After that the professor's rounds took place, and we split into those going to surgery and those going to the ER. The operations were mainly inguinal hernia, GERD, cholecystitis and colorectal cancer, cases that are convincing in this country where many people drink beer, eat meat and are stout, as well as thyroid tumours. Here I was allowed to scrub in as an assistant. In the ER, I attended a single doctor for the most part and saw all kinds of patients together with him, such as a sort of surgical outpatient clinic managing postoperative patients, people with appendicitis or psychiatric diseases, and fractures. When I said I wanted to practise and see ultrasound, I was able to do it and observe it on actual patients. As expected, perhaps because it was a community hospital, I thought I was allowed to do quite a lot. The surgeons here were very good to me, and despite the German-language barrier I was invited to dinner (a beer restaurant, of course), and I was able to spend a very enjoyable and meaningful time.

Next, I rotated for four weeks through orthopedics (trauma surgery) at the university hospital. The rough flow was gathering in the morning, doing ward rounds, going to the conference, and then going to the outpatient clinic or surgery. Here too, although it was a university hospital, the number of doctors was small and I was allowed to scrub in on one or two operations every day. From light ones such as fixation of a radius fracture in an outpatient operating room, to operations for fixation of pelvic fractures from high-energy trauma and spinal surgery, I was allowed to take part, and it was very educational. In the outpatient clinic, I attended the professor of spinal surgery and was allowed to learn neurological examination. I think I was able to learn a lot here as a member of the team, as an assistant in surgery.

Furthermore, at the university hospital I was allowed to rotate through cardiac surgery for one week. Because of the nature of the department I could not scrub in on many operations, so I took part in conferences, attended the professor's lectures and observed surgery. The lectures were quite clinically oriented, and although they were in German and there were things I did not understand because of the language, they seemed very easy to follow. In surgery, valve replacement and implantation of ventricular assist devices seemed to be common. The professor also took me by classic car to Freiburg University's Heart Center (the largest in Europe), where I had very valuable experiences such as scrubbing in on a valve replacement operation.

And finally, I rotated for three weeks through anesthesiology at a community hospital. Here too, each morning we held a conference on surgery and the ICU, after which we went into our respective operations or ran the outpatient clinic. Within that, I mainly observed and assisted with anesthetic management in the operating room, trained in ECG diagnosis, and was allowed to do various procedures at induction (tracheal intubation, lines, NG tubes, ventilator settings). As expected, perhaps because it was a community hospital, I was allowed to experience many procedures, which was very educational. As for cases, I was involved in anesthesia for various operations, starting with general surgery and including orthopedics, breast surgery and obstetrics and gynecology, which was also very educational.

Through this clerkship, by being able to live and train in a place with an environment and culture so different, where one cannot learn much unless one acts proactively or shows one's presence, I naturally became proactive and came to have confidence. Making use of this experience, I was able to develop the spirit to think of making a mark in this field of medicine, which is said to be lifelong study. Also, I will summarise what I thought it would have been good to do in advance regarding the clerkship in Germany during these three months. My study of German was half-done, but it did not trouble me much in the clerkship. However, there were unexpectedly some medical English terms that did not come to me quickly, and this was a big problem. So, for those who go to Germany next time, I would recommend limiting German to what is needed for daily life (self-introduction, ordering at shops, greetings and so on), and studying medical English vocabulary thoroughly.

Finally, I was able to spend such fulfilling three months thanks to the doctors of Nagoya University beginning with Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川, the administrative staff beginning with 西尾-san, the Foreign Office of Freiburg University and the people in each department, and last but certainly not least 桐山-kun, who went to Freiburg University together with me, and others concerned. I would like to take this opportunity to express my deep thanks. Thank you very much indeed.
